passages.happening:
Paul turns to Israel's story. “I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our forefathers were all under the cloud, and that they all passed through the sea” (verse 1).

“They were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (verse 2). They all ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink, “for they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ” (verse 4).

Then comes the blow. “Nevertheless, God was not pleased with most of them, for they were struck down in the wilderness” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Most of the church in Corinth were Gentiles, people who were not Jews. Yet Paul calls the Israelites who left Egypt ‘our forefathers’. Through Christ, Gentile believers have been brought into Israel's family story.

Notice the word ‘all’. Paul says it five times in four verses: all under the cloud, all through the sea, all baptized, all ate, all drank. Every one of them had the same gifts. Then: ‘most of them’ fell. Having the gifts did not keep them.

Why tell this story here? The strong in Corinth felt safe. They had been baptized. They shared the Lord's Supper. They knew idols were nothing. So, they thought, they could eat at a temple dinner without harm. Paul answers with Israel. Israel had its own ‘baptism’ in the sea and its own holy food and drink, and many still fell into idolatry. The signs of God's grace are not a shield that lets you walk into danger.

‘The spiritual rock that accompanied them’ is a puzzle. In Exodus and Numbers water comes from a rock twice, once near the start of the desert years and once near the end. Later Jewish writings tell of a well that travelled with Israel through the desert. Whether that story was already known in Paul's day, and whether he had it in mind, is debated.

‘Spiritual’ here means given by God's Spirit and pointing beyond itself. The manna and the water were real food and drink. They were also God's provision, and Paul sees Christ in them.
passages.ot:
Paul retells the Exodus. “And the LORD went before them in a pillar of cloud to guide their way by day” (Exodus 13:21). Then “the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground” (Exodus 14:22). God gave bread from heaven: “Behold, I will rain down bread from heaven for you” (Exodus 16:4). And water from the rock: “when you strike the rock, water will come out of it for the people to drink” (Exodus 17:6). It happened again years later (Numbers 20:11). A psalm sings of it: “He brought streams from the stone and made water flow down like rivers” (Psalm 78:16).

The Old Testament also calls God himself the Rock. “He is the Rock, His work is perfect; all His ways are just” (Deuteronomy 32:4). That song of Moses is in Paul's mind all through this chapter.

‘Struck down in the wilderness’ recalls how a whole generation died in the desert and did not enter the land (Numbers 14).
passages.hard:
What does Paul mean by ‘that rock was Christ’ (verse 4)?

Readers take it in a few ways. Many read it as saying that Christ was truly present with Israel in the desert, long before he was born as a man. The Old Testament calls God the Rock (Deuteronomy 32:4), and Paul names that Rock as Christ. On this reading the verse is a plain witness that the Son was with his people from the start. Paul says something similar in verse 9: Israel ‘tested Christ’ in the desert. (Some old copies read ‘the Lord’ there; most modern editions print ‘Christ’.)

Others read it more as a picture. The rock that gave water stood for Christ, as later events point back to earlier ones. The Greek word for ‘examples’ in verse 6 is typos, a pattern or stamp, and reading Israel's history as patterns that point to Christ is called typology.

The two readings can sit together. Either way, Paul's point is that Israel's life in the desert came from the same Lord the Corinthians now know, and that Israel still fell.
passages.asks: Israel had every gift and still fell. Ask what you might be counting on to keep you safe: your baptism, your church, your knowledge. Then ask whether you are trusting the Rock himself, or only the gifts he has given.

passages.t: Warnings for us, and a way out
passages.happening:
“These things took place as examples to keep us from craving evil things as they did” (verse 6).

Paul names four warnings. Do not be idolaters: “The people sat down to eat and to drink, and got up to indulge in revelry” (verse 7). Do not commit sexual immorality, as some did, “and in one day twenty-three thousand of them died” (verse 8). Do not test Christ, as some did and were killed by snakes (verse 9). Do not complain, as some did and were killed by the destroying angel (verse 10).

These things “were written down as warnings for us, on whom the fulfillment of the ages has come” (verse 11). “So the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall” (verse 12).

Then a promise. “No temptation has seized you except what is common to man. And God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. But when you are tempted, He will also provide an escape, so that you can stand up under it” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Each warning fit Corinth. The golden calf began with a feast, eating and drinking before an idol, and the Corinthians were eating at the feasts of the gods. The sin at Peor was sexual sin joined to the worship of other gods, and chapter 6 showed that some in Corinth used prostitutes. Testing God and grumbling were the sins of a people who thought they knew better than God.

‘On whom the fulfillment of the ages has come’ means that the church lives at the turning point of history. What God began with Israel has reached its goal in Christ. So Israel's story is not someone else's story. It was written for this church.

Verse 13 uses the word peirasmos. It can mean a test or trial, or a temptation to sin. Here the setting decides. Paul has just named idolatry, sexual sin, testing God and grumbling, and in the next verse he says “flee from idolatry” (verse 14). The pull Paul means is the pull to sin, above all the pull back to the gods' tables.

Paul gives three comforts. The temptation is ‘common to man’: no one faces a pull no one else has faced. God is ‘faithful’: he will not leave his people to it. And God gives ‘an escape’, in Greek ekbasis, a way out. Paul's way out here is plain: flee.
passages.ot:
Paul's four warnings come from Exodus and Numbers. The golden calf: “And the people sat down to eat and drink, and got up to indulge in revelry” (Exodus 32:6), which Paul quotes in verse 7. The sin with the women of Moab at Peor, where the people bowed to their gods (Numbers 25:1-3). The snakes: “So the LORD sent venomous snakes among the people, and many of the Israelites were bitten and died” (Numbers 21:6). The grumbling: “The next day the whole congregation of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron” (Numbers 16:41), followed by a plague.

Numbers gives the dead at Peor as twenty-four thousand: “but those who died in the plague numbered 24,000” (Numbers 25:9). Paul says twenty-three thousand ‘in one day’. Readers have long noticed this. Some think Paul counts those who died in one day, while Numbers counts the whole plague. Others think he gives a round number from memory. His point does not rest on the figure.

A psalm warned later generations in the same way: “do not harden your hearts as you did at Meribah” (Psalm 95:8).
passages.hard:
Does verse 13 mean that God will never give you more than you can handle?

No. That saying is common, and it is often meant kindly, but it is not what this verse says. Verse 13 is about temptation to sin. It promises that God will not let his people be pulled toward sin beyond what they can resist, and that he gives a way out. It is not a promise that God never lets a person carry more suffering, grief or pain than they can bear on their own.

Paul himself said the opposite about suffering. He told the same church, “We were under a burden far beyond our ability to endure, so that we despaired even of life” (2 Corinthians 1:8). He did not say the burden was small. He said it taught him to trust “in God, who raises the dead” (2 Corinthians 1:9).

So if your life is more than you can carry, that does not mean you are weak or that your faith has failed. People are not meant to carry it alone. The psalm says, “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18). Tell someone you trust: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. If you are thinking of ending your life, or you are in danger, get help now; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Nor does the verse mean God is the one tempting you. “God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone” (James 1:13).
passages.asks: ‘The one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall.’ Ask where you feel most sure of yourself. Then ask what your ‘way out’ looks like when temptation comes: who you can call, where you can go, what you need to walk away from.

passages.t: The table of the Lord and the table of demons
passages.happening:
“Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry” (verse 14). Paul asks them to judge for themselves (verse 15).

“Is not the cup of blessing that we bless a participation in the blood of Christ? And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ?” (verse 16). “Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf” (verse 17).

Look at Israel: those who eat the sacrifices share in the altar (verse 18). Is Paul saying an idol is anything? “No, but the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons, not to God. And I do not want you to be participants with demons” (verse 20).

“You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too; you cannot partake in the table of the Lord and the table of demons too” (verse 21). “Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than He?” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
In the Greek and Roman world a sacrifice usually ended in a meal. Part of the animal was burned for the god, and the rest was eaten, often in dining rooms at the temple, with the god treated as host. An invitation from Roman Egypt asks a guest to dine ‘at the table of the lord Sarapis’. So ‘the table of demons’ was not a strange phrase. It was the plain language of a temple dinner turned round.

‘Participation’ is koinōnia: sharing, fellowship, having a part in something together. It is where the word ‘communion’ comes from. To eat at a table is to share in what the table stands for. At the Lord's table believers share in Christ. At an idol's table, Paul says, people share with the powers behind the idol.

‘The cup of blessing’ was a cup over which thanks to God was said. Later Jewish writings use the same name for the cup of wine after the grace at the end of a meal, and at Passover for the third of four cups. Paul's phrase may echo that custom; how far back it goes is not certain.

Verse 17 says something the next chapter will press hard. One loaf, one body. To eat the one bread is to be joined to every other believer who eats it. Chapter 11 will show the Corinthians breaking that body apart at the very table that should join them.

Paul still holds what he said in chapter 8: an idol is nothing. But behind the worship of idols, he says, are real spiritual powers opposed to God. Knowing the idol is nothing does not make it safe to eat at its feast.
passages.ot:
Paul's words come almost straight from the song of Moses: “They sacrificed to demons, not to God, to gods they had not known” (Deuteronomy 32:17). A psalm says the same: “They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons” (Psalm 106:37).

‘Provoke the Lord to jealousy’ also comes from that song: “They have provoked My jealousy by that which is not God; they have enraged Me with their worthless idols” (Deuteronomy 32:21). God's jealousy is not petty. It is the love of a husband who will not share his bride. “For you must not worship any other god, for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God” (Exodus 34:14).

Israel's priests and worshippers ate parts of the sacrifices. “The meat of the sacrifice of his peace offering of thanksgiving must be eaten on the day he offers it” (Leviticus 7:15). Eating from the altar meant sharing in the worship.
passages.hard:
What does ‘participation in the blood of Christ’ say about the Lord's Supper?

At the least it says the Supper is more than a reminder. Those who eat and drink share in Christ and in the benefits of his death, and are joined to one another as one body. Beyond that, churches understand Christ's presence in the meal in different ways. The notes on chapter 11, where Paul tells of the night Jesus gave the meal, set out those views.

Are demons real? Paul says the gods were nothing as gods, and that real evil powers stood behind their worship. Christians across the centuries have read him this way. These notes do not make claims about any modern religion or person. Paul's concern is the believer who joins in worship given to another god.
passages.asks: Paul says no one can sit at two tables. Ask what ‘tables’ you sit at: the places where you give your loyalty, your time and your worship. And when you take the bread and cup, ask who else you are joined to by that one loaf.

passages.t: ‘Do it all to the glory of God’
passages.happening:
Paul quotes the Corinthian saying again. “Everything is permissible,” but not everything is beneficial. “Everything is permissible,” but not everything is edifying (verse 23). “No one should seek his own good, but the good of others” (verse 24).

Then practical answers. Eat anything sold in the meat market without asking questions of conscience, because the earth and everything in it belong to the Lord (verses 25-26). If an unbeliever invites you to a meal and you want to go, eat whatever is served, without asking (verse 27).

But if someone tells you, “This food was offered to idols,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who told you and for conscience' sake: his conscience, not yours (verses 28-29).

“So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God” (verse 31). Give no cause to stumble to Jews, Greeks or the church of God (verse 32). Paul tries to please everyone in all he does, not seeking his own good, “but the good of many, that they may be saved” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
The meat market, makellon in Greek, macellum in Latin, was the city's food market, where meat was sold. Some meat there had come from sacrifices, and some had not, and a buyer often could not tell. Paul says: do not ask. The food itself is God's.

A private dinner in an unbeliever's home was different from a feast in a temple. Paul does not tell believers to refuse their neighbours' invitations. Eat, and give thanks.

But if someone at the table says, ‘This was offered to idols’, the meal now says something. The one who spoke, perhaps a fellow guest with a tender conscience, perhaps the pagan host himself, will watch what the believer does. To eat then would look like joining in the god's honour. So Paul says leave it, for the other person's sake.

Paul has now given three answers on food offered to idols. Never join in a feast of the gods (verses 14-22). Buy and eat freely at the market and at a neighbour's table (verses 25-27). Give up even that freedom when someone else's faith or understanding is at stake (verses 28-29).

Verse 31 gathers it all. Eating and drinking are not outside the Christian life. Ordinary meals, work and rest can all be done for God's honour.
passages.ot:
Paul's ground for eating freely is a psalm: “The earth is the LORD’s, and the fullness thereof, the world and all who dwell therein” (Psalm 24:1). Everything good comes from God, including the meat in the market. Paul says the same elsewhere: “For every creation of God is good, and nothing that is received with thanksgiving should be rejected” (1 Timothy 4:4).

The Old Testament also knows the duty not to trip up another. “You must not curse the deaf or place a stumbling block before the blind” (Leviticus 19:14), which the notes on chapter 8 quote.
passages.asks: Paul says that even eating and drinking can be done for God's glory. Pick one ordinary thing you will do tomorrow: a meal, a task, a conversation. Ask what it would look like to do it for God's honour and for someone else's good, and not only your own.
